notes.front: What is a packing group (PG)?
notes.explanation: Within one hazard class, the packing group says how dangerous a particular material is.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Packing group”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Packing group means a grouping according to the degree of danger presented by hazardous materials.
notes.back: A grouping of hazardous materials according to the degree of danger they present.
notes.example: Like a severity grade on a warning: the same class, but graded I, II or III.

notes.front: What is a hazard zone?
notes.explanation: Hazard zones grade inhalation toxicity, much as packing groups grade danger in general.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Hazard zone”, p. 27
notes.evidence: Hazard zone means one of four levels of hazard (Hazard Zones A through D) assigned to gases, as specified in § 173.116(a) of this subchapter, and one of two levels of hazards (Hazard Zones A and B) assigned to liquids that are poisonous by inhalation
notes.back: One of four levels (Zones A to D) for gases, or one of two levels (Zones A and B) for liquids poisonous by inhalation.
notes.example: Like a packing group, but only for inhalation toxicity, and lettered rather than numbered.

notes.front: Packing Group I indicates {{c1::great}} danger.
notes.explanation: The numbering runs from the most dangerous group (I) down to the least dangerous (III).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Packing group”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Packing Group I indicates great danger; Packing Group II, medium danger; Packing Group III, minor danger.

notes.front: Packing Group II indicates {{c1::medium}} danger.
notes.explanation: It sits between Packing Group I (great danger) and Packing Group III (minor danger).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Packing group”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Packing Group I indicates great danger; Packing Group II, medium danger; Packing Group III, minor danger.

notes.front: Packing Group III indicates {{c1::minor}} danger.
notes.explanation: The highest number is the lowest danger, so PG III is the least dangerous group.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Packing group”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Packing Group I indicates great danger; Packing Group II, medium danger; Packing Group III, minor danger.

notes.front: Which classes or divisions have no packing groups?
notes.explanation: The same paragraph adds that articles outside Class 1 have no packing group either.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(f), p. 7
notes.evidence: Class 2, Class 7, and Division 6.2 do not have packing groups.

notes.front: Are articles assigned to packing groups?
notes.explanation: For packing purposes, any packaging performance level they need is set in the packing authorizations of part 173.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(f), p. 7
notes.evidence: Articles in classes other than Class 1 are not assigned to packing groups. For packing purposes, any requirement for a specific packaging performance level is set out in the applicable packing authorizations of part 173.
notes.back: Only in Class 1. Articles in any other class are not assigned to packing groups.

notes.front: Where is a material's packing group found, and what decides it when more than one is shown?
notes.explanation: Subpart D holds the packing group criteria for each class, such as flash point and boiling point for Class 3.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(f), p. 7
notes.evidence: If more than one packing group is indicated for an entry, the packing group for the hazardous material is determined using the criteria for assignment of packing groups specified in subpart D of part 173.
notes.back: Column 5 of the § 172.101 table; when several are shown, the criteria in subpart D of part 173.

notes.front: Which Class 3 liquids go in Packing Group I?
notes.explanation: The Class 3 criteria table gives no flash point limit for PG I, only the boiling point.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.121(a)(1), p. 108
notes.evidence: When the § 172.101 Table provides more than one packing group for a hazardous material, the packing group must be determined by applying the following criteria:
notes.back: Those with an initial boiling point of 35 °C (95 °F) or less, whatever the flash point.

notes.front: Which Class 3 liquids go in Packing Group II?
notes.explanation: Both columns of the Class 3 criteria table must be read together.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.121(a)(1), p. 108
notes.evidence: When the § 172.101 Table provides more than one packing group for a hazardous material, the packing group must be determined by applying the following criteria:
notes.back: Flash point (closed-cup) below 23 °C (73 °F) and initial boiling point above 35 °C (95 °F).

notes.front: Which Class 3 liquids go in Packing Group III?
notes.explanation: The top of this band is the 60 °C limit of Class 3 itself.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.121(a)(1), p. 108
notes.evidence: When the § 172.101 Table provides more than one packing group for a hazardous material, the packing group must be determined by applying the following criteria:
notes.back: Flash point 23 °C to 60 °C inclusive (73 °F to 140 °F) and initial boiling point above 35 °C (95 °F).

notes.front: A hazard zone is based on the {{c1::LC50}} value for acute inhalation toxicity of gases and vapours.
notes.explanation: LC50 is the concentration in air that kills half of the test animals, so the lower the LC50, the more toxic the material and the nearer it is to Zone A.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Hazard zone”, p. 27
notes.evidence: A hazard zone is based on the LC50 value for acute inhalation toxicity of gases and vapors, as specified in § 173.133(a).
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation

notes.front: Which gas divisions have no hazard zones?
notes.explanation: Hazard zones are assigned only to Division 2.3 gases, in column 7 of the § 172.101 table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.116(a), p. 106
notes.evidence: The hazard zone of a Class 2, Division 2.3 material is assigned in column 7 of the § 172.101 table. There are no hazard zones for Divisions 2.1 and 2.2.

notes.front: A Division 2.3 gas is in Hazard Zone A when its LC50 is {{c1::less than or equal to 200 ppm}}.
notes.explanation: Zone A is the most toxic band, so it has the lowest limit; Zones B, C and D have upper limits of 1000, 3000 and 5000 ppm.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.116(a), p. 106
notes.evidence: LC50 less than or equal to 200 ppm. LC50 greater than 200 ppm and less than or equal to 1000 ppm.
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation

notes.front: Under § 173.133, what is a Division 6.1 liquid that meets the Packing Group I, Hazard Zone A or B criteria for vapour inhalation?
notes.explanation: Note 2 to the Division 6.1 vapour table ties these zones to the inhalation hazard rules.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.133(a)(2), note 2, p. 117
notes.evidence: A liquid in Division 6.1 meeting criteria for Packing Group I, Hazard Zones A or B stated in paragraph (a)(2) of this section is a material poisonous by inhalation subject to the additional hazard communication requirements
notes.back: A material poisonous by inhalation, subject to additional hazard communication requirements.

notes.front: On a United Nations standard packaging mark, what does the performance letter X mean?
notes.explanation: The letter tells which packing groups' tests the packaging design type has passed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 178 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 178.503(a)(3), p. 190
notes.evidence: X—for packagings meeting Packing Group I, II and III tests;
notes.back: The design type passed the tests for Packing Groups I, II and III.

notes.front: On a United Nations standard packaging mark, what does the performance letter Z mean?
notes.explanation: Z is the lowest of the three performance levels, matching the minor danger group.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 178 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 178.503(a)(3), p. 190
notes.evidence: Z—for packagings only meeting Packing Group III tests;
notes.back: The design type passed only the Packing Group III tests.

notes.front: When a material has several hazards with different packing groups, which packing group does it take?
notes.explanation: The note gives the example of Class 3 PG II with Division 6.1 PG I (oral), which becomes Class 3 PG I.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(b), note 1, p. 7
notes.evidence: The most stringent packing group assigned to a hazard of the material takes precedence over other packing groups;
notes.back: The most stringent packing group assigned to any of its hazards.

notes.front: A liquid has a closed-cup flash point of 10 °C and an initial boiling point of 80 °C. The § 172.101 table shows more than one packing group for it. Which applies?
notes.explanation: A flash point below 23 °C with a boiling point above 35 °C is the PG II row.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.121(a)(1), p. 108
notes.evidence: When the § 172.101 Table provides more than one packing group for a hazardous material, the packing group must be determined by applying the following criteria:
notes.choices:
A) PG I
B) PG II
C) PG III
D) None: Class 3 has no packing groups
notes.choicesExplained: A: PG I needs an initial boiling point of 35 °C or less. C: PG III needs a flash point of at least 23 °C. D: only Class 2, Class 7 and Division 6.2 lack packing groups.

notes.front: A shipper must enter a packing group for each of four materials. For which one will the § 172.101 table show no packing group?
notes.explanation: Class 2, Class 7 and Division 6.2 have no packing groups.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(f), p. 7
notes.evidence: Class 2, Class 7, and Division 6.2 do not have packing groups.
notes.choices:
A) A Class 8 liquid
B) A Division 6.1 solid
C) A Class 3 liquid
D) A Division 2.2 compressed gas
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 8 materials are assigned packing groups. B: Division 6.1 materials are assigned packing groups. C: Class 3 materials are assigned packing groups.

notes.front: A Division 2.3 gas has an LC50 of 150 ppm, and the § 172.101 table leaves its hazard zone to the criteria. Which zone applies?
notes.explanation: An LC50 of 200 ppm or less is Zone A.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.116(a), p. 106
notes.evidence: LC50 less than or equal to 200 ppm. LC50 greater than 200 ppm and less than or equal to 1000 ppm.
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.choices:
A) Hazard Zone A
B) Hazard Zone B
C) Hazard Zone D
D) No zone: gases have no hazard zones
notes.choicesExplained: B: Zone B starts above 200 ppm. C: Zone D covers LC50 values above 3000 ppm, up to 5000 ppm. D: Division 2.3 gases are assigned hazard zones; only Divisions 2.1 and 2.2 have none.

notes.front: A drum's United Nations standard mark carries the performance letter Y. Which packing groups' tests has its design type passed?
notes.explanation: Y sits between X and Z, covering the medium and minor danger groups.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 178 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 178.503(a)(3), p. 190
notes.evidence: Y—for packagings meeting Packing Group II and III tests; or
notes.back: C: Packing Groups II and III
notes.choices:
A) Packing Groups I, II and III
B) Packing Group III only
C) Packing Groups II and III
D) Packing Group I only
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the letter X. B: that is the letter Z. D: no performance letter covers PG I alone; X covers I, II and III.

notes.front: A liquid not listed by name meets Class 3 at PG III and Division 6.1 at PG II (oral). The precedence table ranks Division 6.1 above Class 3 for this pair. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: The table picks the class, and note 1 gives the most stringent packing group of the material's hazards.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(b), note 1, p. 7
notes.evidence: The most stringent packing group assigned to a hazard of the material takes precedence over other packing groups;
notes.choices:
A) Class 3, PG III
B) Class 3, PG II
C) Division 6.1, PG II
D) Division 6.1, PG III
notes.choicesExplained: A: the precedence table gives Division 6.1 for this pair, and PG II is the more stringent group. B: the class comes from the precedence table, which gives Division 6.1 here. D: the most stringent packing group takes precedence, and that is PG II.
